extracted.intended_audience: Citizens of New York and the general public considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of Federalist essays (Nos. 25–29) arguing how the national government should be empowered to provide for common defense, balance standing armies and militias, and how legislative restraints and institutional design check abuses of military power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for a regular disciplined military for effective war operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The steady operations of war against a regular and disciplined army can only be successfully conducted by a force of the same kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia valor is acknowledged, but the militia alone could not have established or maintained national liberty in prolonged conventional war; war is a science requiring diligence, perseverance, time, and practice. Policymakers should recognize that certain military functions require regularly trained, disciplined forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impracticable constitutional prohibitions on military establishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Fettering the government with restrictions that cannot be observed is unwise; parchment provisions are unequal to a struggle with public necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State provisions that declare standing armies 'ought not to be kept up' are ambiguous and likely to be treated as admonitions rather than prohibitions when necessity arises. Laws or constitutional clauses that aim at absolute exclusion of measures needed in emergencies will be disregarded and undermine respect for fundamental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit appropriations to force periodic legislative review
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrain appropriations of money for military purposes to the period of two years so the legislature must periodically deliberate on maintaining a standing military.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biennial appropriations compel the legislature to publicly re-examine and vote on military support at least every two years; this keeps public attention focused, invites opposition critique, and enables state legislatures and the people to check excesses before permanent funds are vested in the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative oversight and periodic public debate as checks on military abuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent legislative debate and the potential for opposition and state-level vigilance will warn the community if the majority seeks to exceed proper limits on military power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because appropriations recur, party opposition can rouse public attention; state legislatures act as jealous guardians and can sound the alarm. Regular public votes on military funding help prevent gradual, concealed accumulation of forces that could threaten liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trade the risk of executive misuse for paralysis of government
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to hazard the abuse of confidence placed in the legislature than to embarrass the government and endanger public safety by imprudent restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete exclusion of necessary powers (for defense/public security) risks incapacitating government in crises; designers should prefer accountable authority with checks rather than rigid bans that impede necessary action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality and enforceability of constitutional language matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguous or unnecessary declarations (e.g., 'ought not' vs 'shall not') produce little efficacy; provisions must be framed to effect salutary operation without imprudent extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The English Bill of Rights forbade standing armies 'unless with the consent of Parliament'—that restrained executive power without hamstringing the legislature. Provisions should avoid aims that either do too much or are unenforceable in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: National regulation of militia for uniformity and effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformity in the organization and discipline of the militia would produce the most beneficial effects when called into service for public defense; this uniformity can only be accomplished by confiding regulation to the national authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed plan empowers the Union 'to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia,' while reserving to the states the appointment of officers and training according to the discipline prescribed by Congress. Central regulation facilitates mutual intelligence and concert in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of force: militia for small disturbances, regular forces for major insurrections
rubrics_metrics.description: If a commotion is slight and localized, the militia should suffice; if an insurrection pervades a whole State, a different, more regular force may become unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Massachusetts, Pennsylvania) show states raising troops for internal disorders. Policymakers should allow the national government the means to employ the appropriate kind and scale of force proportional to the emergency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity and scope of federal authority reduce need for coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the operations of the national authority are intermingled in ordinary governance, the more familiar citizens become with it and the less likely it will have to recur to force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending federal authority to internal matters brings government into common life, building respect and attachment; a government continually distant is less able to command voluntary obedience and more likely to resort to violent expedients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral and institutional rotation check long-term conspiracies to seize power
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes to subvert liberties require time to mature; biennial elections and representative rotation make it improbable that sustained conspiracies between legislature and executive would persist across successive bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequent changes in legislative composition increase the chance that at least some members will detect and expose conspiracies; if conspiracies are improbable and concealment impracticable, fears of inevitable usurpation are overstated.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments as mutual checks on federal encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures and governments will act as vigilant guardians and auxiliaries to resist federal encroachments and to serve as instruments of redress for the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because federal laws become supreme only within constitutional bounds, state officers (legislatures, courts, magistrates) are incorporated into national operations as far as federal authority extends; states can coordinate and combine resources to check excesses of the federal government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic extent and resources of the nation are safeguards against federal tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: The great extent of country and distributed population make it difficult for a federal government to raise and maintain an army able to subdue the liberties of a vast people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistics and limited resources initially constrain federal military size; even if a federal army suppressed resistance in one place, distant states could raise fresh forces. Designers should consider size and resource limits as structural protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reliance on theoretical doctrines that ignore empirical experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that government can be at all times governed by law alone is a reverie; seditions and insurrections sometimes make force necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design and policy should be informed by historical experience (domestic and foreign) and practical contingencies rather than abstract dogma that forbids any use of force under all circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impractical restraints produce precedents for breaches and erode reverence for the constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Every breach of fundamental laws, though dictated by necessity, impairs sacred reverence toward the constitution and forms precedents for other breaches where necessity is less urgent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should craft provisions that are manageable and observeable; otherwise, necessity will compel breaches that weaken constitutional authority and promote future abuses.
